The schoolhouse stood at the end of a dirt road, a single room with a stove in the middle and a bell on a post outside. In the morning the children arrived on foot, some of them having walked three miles, and took their places on benches worn smooth by earlier generations. I was struck, as I watched them, by the seriousness with which they approached their lessons; for them an education was not an entitlement but a hard-won chance. Their parents, who had little schooling themselves, had built the place with their own hands and paid the teacher out of meager harvests. In that single room, I thought, was the whole argument for public education: that a people who invest in their children’s minds invest in their own future, however poor they may be today.
